judge.e: From Middle English juge, jugge, from Old French juge, from Latin iūdex.
judge.g: A public official whose duty it is to administer the law, especially by presiding over trials and rendering judgments; a justice.

judge.e: From Middle English jugen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman juger, from Old French jugier, from Latin iūdicāre. Partly displaced native deem.
judge.g: To sit in judgment on; to pass sentence on (a person or matter).

judgment.e: From Middle English juggement, borrowed from Old French jugement, from Late Latin iūdicāmentum, from Latin iūdicō. Partially displaced doom. By surface analysis, judge + -ment.

jug.e: From Middle English jugge, of uncertain origin. Possibly a variant of Middle English jubbe, jobbe, iubbe, geobbe, itself of unknown origin; or perhaps continuing (in altered form) Old English ċēac (“pitcher; jug”). Prison sense attested from at least 1825 in Britain.
jug.g: A serving vessel or container, typically circular in cross-section and typically higher than it is wide, with a relatively small mouth or sp
A small mixed breed of dog created by mating a Jack Russell terrier and a pug.

juice.e: From Middle English jus, juis, from Old French jus, jous, from Latin jūs (“broth, soup, sauce”), from Proto-Indo-European *yéwHs, from *yewH- (“to mix (of meal preparation)”). In this sense, mostly displaced native Middle English sew (“juice”), from Old English sēaw (“juice, sap”) (> English sew (“juice, broth, gravy”)).
juice.g: A liquid made from plant, especially fruit.

juice.e: Dialectal spelling of Jew's, a particle of unclear origin.
juice.g: Alternative spelling of Jew's (used in certain set phrases like juice harp)

jump.e: From Middle English jumpen (“to walk quickly, run, jump”), probably of Middle Low German or North Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *gumpōną ~ *gumbōną (“to hop, skip, bounce”), an iterative verb. The OED suggests an imitative origin.
jump.g: To propel oneself rapidly upward, downward and/or in any horizontal direction such that momentum causes the body to become airborne.

junction.e: From Latin iūnctiō (“union, joining, uniting”), from iungō (“join, attach together”). Equivalent to join + -tion.
junction.g: The act of joining, or the state of being joined.

juniper.e: From Late Middle English junyper, juniperus, from Latin iūniperus (“juniper-tree”).
juniper.g: Any shrub or tree of the genus Juniperus of the cypress family, which is characterized by pointed, needle-like leaves and aromatic berry-lik

jurisdiction.g: The power, right, or authority to interpret and apply the law.

just.e: From Middle English juste, from Old French juste, from Latin iūstus (“just, lawful, rightful, true, due, proper, moderate”), from Proto-Italic *jowestos, related to Latin iūs (“law, right”); ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yew-.
Variation of joust, presumably ultimately from Latin iuxta (“near, besides”).

justice.e: From Middle English justice, from Old French justise, justice (Modern French justice), from Latin iūstitia (“righteousness, equity”), from iūstus (“just”), from iūs (“right”), from Proto-Italic *jowos, perhaps literally "sacred formula", a word peculiar to Latin (not general Italic) that originated in the religious cults, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yew-.
justice.g: The state or characteristic of being just or fair.

justification.e: From Middle English justificacioun, justification, from Middle French justification, from Late Latin iustificationem, justificationem < iustificatio, from iustifico, from Latin iustus.
justification.g: A reason, explanation, or excuse which someone believes provides convincing, morally acceptable support for behavior or for a belief or occu

justifier.g: One who, or that which, justifies some belief or action.

justify.e: From Middle English justifien, from Old French justifier, from Late Latin justificare (“make just”), from Latin justus, iustus (“just”) + ficare (“make”), from facere, equivalent to just + -ify.
justify.g: To provide an acceptable explanation for.

jut.e: From Middle English jutten (“to project, jut out”), an alteration of jetten (“to strut, be showy”).
